Roadmap

Source: Roadmap.md

What is deliberately not built yet, and the reasoning already settled about it. Design decisions recorded here are conclusions, not opinions to re-litigate — several were reached by building the alternative first.

For what the package is, see the README and vignette("plan_concepts").

Agentic planner: responsibility split

The package’s next job is to be the substrate an agentic media planner works on: an agent inspects a plan compactly, acts on it only through validated ops, never violates a commercial commitment, is scored by mrmopt at the right grain, checks itself against the same constraints the optimizer uses, and leaves an auditable record of what it changed and why.

Three owners, one job each:

  • mediaplanr — plan state, legal actions, constraints, checks, history.
  • mrmopt — scoring and optimization.
  • The app — the agent loop and the human approval gate.

The loop this supports, and which step each owner takes:

describe        describe_plan(plan)                         mediaplanr
propose ops     op_*() / JSON against plan_ops_schema(plan) agent (app)
validate        build_scenario(plan, edits, rationale = )   mediaplanr
score           spend_by_model() -> response models         mrmopt
check           check_constraints(scenario, constraints)    mediaplanr
record why      @rationale, edit_log()                      mediaplanr
approve         revise(status = "approved")                 human (app)

Much of this is already in place, and it is the reason the package suits the job: value semantics, a validator on every construction, ops as data, errors that list the alternatives, lineage and status. An agent cannot corrupt a plan, and every proposal it makes is an inspectable scenario rather than an edit in place.

What was missing, and its status:

  1. Commitments the edit path respects — row-level spend bounds, so money that cannot move is a fact in the plan rather than something an agent has to be told. Built in 0.2.0.
  2. A compact, bounded plan summary for the agent’s context — describe_plan(). Built in 0.2.0.
  3. A deterministic map from line items to mrmopt response models, which may be fitted at a different (and mixed) grain — model_map(), spend_by_model(). Built in 0.3.0.
  4. One constraint object read by both the agent’s self-check and the optimizer — PlanConstraints, check_constraints(). Built in 0.3.0.
  5. Structured rationale on each proposal — who proposed it, toward what goal, under which constraints. Built in 0.2.0, as @rationale.

The agent loop itself is the app’s, not this package’s; vignette("agentic_planning") runs one turn of it with real calls.

Sections and scopes

Built in 0.4.0. A client keeps one master plan per fiscal year, worked on by several planners at once. The client’s organization – brand and performance, lines of business, channels – is a tree of sections, and each planner is scoped to some of them.

Decided

  • A section is a target: the same named list of grain columns and values an op, a check_budget() row and a PlanConstraints rule already use. A scope is a list of targets. A section’s envelope is a check_budget() row. Nothing new is stored.
  • A draft is a scenario under a base revision. It is approved by replaying its @edits on the current revision, so approved revisions stay one chain and current_approved() returns one plan. rebase_check() says whether the replay does what the draft did.
  • Every organization level is a grain column, because a target may only name grain columns. A grouping the plan lacks (funnel over channel) is added with regrain(), which keeps the plan’s id, lineage and approval.
  • The app does not match rows itself. match_rows(), ops_within() and the rest resolve rows through the matcher the edits use, so a scope check cannot disagree with what an edit would touch. They read: they do not refuse subplan-owned rows the way every edit door still does.

API style

Decided

The consumers of the edit path are LLM agents — emitting JSON tool calls or generating R — and the humans reviewing what they did. That decides the style.

In:

  • Plan-first arguments, and pure functions that return the same class.
  • Standard evaluation: column names are strings, targets are named lists (list(channel = "TV")).
  • op_*() constructors, each returning the same plain list a hand-written or JSON-parsed op is, so the three are interchangeable.
  • One JSON Schema for the edits array, plan_ops_schema().

Out, with reasons:

  • dplyr generics on MediaPlan (mutate(), filter(), …). They would bypass everything that makes an edit legal: the validator, the units identity, subplan locks, flight identity and spend bounds. Each would have to re-route through the op machinery anyway, at which point it is an op with a misleading name.
  • Tidy evaluation / bare column names. A quoted R expression is not JSON-serializable, so a tool-calling agent cannot produce one. A target has to be data.
  • Per-step mutating pipe verbs (plan |> scale_spend() |> shift()). Each step would mint a lineage generation, so one intent would land as a chain of half-finished scenarios. One intent is one build_scenario() call with an edits list.

Read-only projections may be piped freely — roll_up(), calendarize(), line_item_summary() and the like return views, not new generations.

SubPlans

Built — attach_subplan(), detach_subplan(), is_topline(), revise(); see Already grown. The design record stays here because the decisions were argued, not assumed.

Status: held. Built and tested at one level. No further investment — no depth testing, no staleness detection — and not exposed in the app until a real multi-owner engagement needs it. The common case that looks like a subplan is a signed budget envelope (channel × quarter authorizations checked with a tolerated variance); that is check_budget(), not ownership.

Known gaps, left as part of the hold: the validator’s subplan invariant compares spend, not spend bounds; and attaching a subplan replaces the cell’s bounds with the subplan’s rollup, so a floor set on the topline cell is dropped if the subplan carries none.

A channel team plans its own detail, at its own granularity, on its own schedule, with its own objectives — and that detail rolls up into the weekly plan everyone else looks at.

MediaPlan  "Q2 2026 Brand Plan"      the topline: channel + week, weekly
  └─ subplan "TV"                    campaign + partner + daypart, daily

Decided

A subplan is a MediaPlan. Composition, not inheritance. S7 supports inheritance, so this is a choice. Two things decide it. First, “subplan” is a property of the relationship, not the object: in a master → TV → NBC nesting the TV plan is a subplan and a topline at once, which a class hierarchy cannot express without the same object being two types. Second, a SubPlan class would add no behaviour — build_scenario(), roll_up(), calendarize() and flights() all do what they already do. What changes is the parent’s behaviour. The package already answers this one level up: ScenarioSet contains MediaPlans rather than subclassing anything.

So this adds one slot and no class:

subplans = S7::new_property(S7::class_list, default = quote(list()))
# names are parent line item keys; values are MediaPlans

“Topline” is prose, not a type. is_topline(plan) is a derived predicate — true when @subplans is non-empty — in the same discipline as flight_window(), week_start() and pacing. A plan does not become a different kind of thing when something is attached beneath it.

Naming. subplan in code, topline in prose. Rejected: channel_plan privileges a column name the package refuses to privilege anywhere (there is no channels(), deliberately, and the nesting axis may be market or brand); schedule reads as a timing concept in a package full of them, and understates a thing carrying its own goals and revisions; buy is already spent — the docs use it throughout to mean a flight.

The subplan owns its numbers. attach_subplan() replaces the parent’s rows for that line item with the subplan’s rollup — weeks the subplan does not plan disappear, weeks it adds appear — so there is one number with one owner. Parent rows backed by a subplan become read-only, and an op reaching one errors naming the right door — “channel TV is planned in a subplan; edit the subplan and re-attach.” A whole-plan op such as total = 200 therefore errors on a topline, deliberately. detach_subplan() leaves the last reconciled numbers as ordinary editable rows, so detaching is never destructive.

Re-attaching is the reconcile; there is no reconcile(). An earlier draft had one. It was dropped as redundant: with value semantics nothing changes behind the caller’s back, so the only way the parent and subplan can disagree is a subplan edited after it was attached — and the fix for that is attaching it again. What makes this safe is a validator invariant: the parent’s rows at each backed cell must equal that subplan’s rollup, checked on every construction and on @<-. Assigning a mismatched subplan straight into the slot is refused, not merely discouraged.

Same grain or finer, and the data declares the cell. A subplan’s line item grain must contain its parent’s — parent keyed channel, subplan keyed channel + partner + daypart, with channel constant at the attached cell. roll_up() already requires its target grain to be a subset of the plan’s, so a superset-grained subplan rolls up to its parent through the aggregation as written. The parent’s key columns are carried in the subplan’s data, not implied by an attachment name, so attach_subplan(parent, subplan) takes no key: the cell is one distinct combination across line_item_grain(parent), a fact in the table rather than a string to parse. Same-grain subplans are allowed — ownership without refinement.

Cadence is the second axis. A weekly parent needs a subplan with a week column; calendarize(subplan, "week", week_start = week_start(parent)) re-cuts its days onto the parent’s weeks before the rollup, so daily flights and a different week start land correctly. A parent whose weeks do not share a weekday cannot host one. A parent keyed by moments has no calendar to gather a subplan onto, and refuses.

Depth is legal; one level is built and tested. A subplan is a MediaPlan, so it carries @subplans too, and master → TV → NBC costs nothing to permit. Reconciliation is local — attaching NBC makes TV’s row right, attaching that TV makes the master’s row right — so no machinery cares about depth. What depth costs is staleness a planner cannot see; detecting it is a check, not a cascade, and it is not built. A plan cannot be attached beneath itself: S7’s value semantics make an object cycle impossible to form, so the rule is an id check — the parent’s id must not appear among the subplan’s descendants.

Campaigns need no new machinery. A campaign is a grain column in the subplan, ordered coarsest-first exactly as roll_up() already expects. That is the payoff of the configurable grain, and the reason this is smaller than it looks.

A subplan carries its own grain and schedule. It is a full MediaPlan, so it need not share the parent’s grain or cadence: a daily channel + partner + daypart plan can sit beneath a weekly channel + week topline, and a channel + market plan can refine a national cell into markets. roll_up() collapses the extra dimensions and calendarize() bridges the cadence, so the subplan reconciles to the single parent cell it backs. The one rule is that everything in the subplan must roll up to that cell — refining a cell, never spanning several.

Revisions. Superseded — see Already grown, Approvals. Planners say Rev 2, so the slot was @revision (integer, default 1), set by hand. It turned out to be the opposite of what a planner means: it reset to 1 on every derivation, while “Rev 2” means “the second approved version” of a plan that was derived many times. The slot was removed; a revision is now derived by lineage() from approvals along the branch.

revise() landed with it

@subplans was the first genuinely new slot since MediaPlan was written, and it walked into a known trap. A consumer that rebuilds a plan by naming its slots by hand — as the MVP app does in set_status_tool, naming eleven — silently drops any slot added later. Changing a scenario’s status would quietly detach every subplan. That is data loss, not cosmetics.

revise(plan, ...) is the metadata-only edit verb that closes it: same @id, only the named fields change, and it refuses anything that is not metadata. Inside the package, .copy_plan() is the one door through which a plan is copied — it reads the settable properties off the class, so a new slot is carried by default and dropped only on purpose. roll_up() drops subplans (a coarser view owns nothing); build_scenario() carries them. The three constructor sites that used to name every slot by hand now go through it.

revise() now sets approval (status and approved_on) rather than a revision number. Note for the app: set_status_tool names slots by hand and may still name revision, which no longer exists; it should call revise().

National and local: geo is a grain, not a feature

A plan is national or local by what it keys on, not by any switch. National is a plan with no geo column; local adds one — market, region, dma, whatever the client calls it — exactly as channel is a dimension a user happened to key on. Everything already follows: roll_up() collapses market -> national, grain_values() lists the markets, and an op can target one. A geo hierarchy (DMA -> region -> national) is coarsest-first grain ordering, which roll_up() already treats as nesting.

So geo needs no new machinery. It arrives on the same two mechanisms channels do, and which one fits is a property of the engagement, not the package:

  • A dimension in one plan — national planners breaking spend down by market: one owner, one artifact. Supported today.
  • An owned subplan — a regional team authoring its market at its own grain and schedule, rolling up into the national topline. This is the SubPlans work above, nesting on market instead of channel; the mechanism is already axis-agnostic (“the nesting axis may be market or brand”).

Decided

No geo taxonomy. The same rule as the channel-type registry: the package ships no canonical list of DMAs, regions or markets, and no built-in geo hierarchy. A market is a dimension the user keyed on; the client’s own naming is the only naming.

The consuming application

The package has grown a good deal that mediaplanr-mvp-app does not yet know about. Its agent tools and system prompt currently describe spend edits on weekly rows and nothing else:

  • Flights. media_plan_from_flights(), flights(), and the fact that a plan can be authored as buys rather than weeks.
  • Structural ops. add, drop, shift, restage and during targeting — the app cannot yet let a planner introduce or remove a line item through chat.
  • Units. unit_type, planned_units, planned_rate, and the “any two give the third” authoring rule at upload.
  • calendarize(). Monthly and daily views, which is what finance asks for.
  • Since 0.2.0. transfer and rebound; spend bounds and the refusals they produce; @rationale (the app should pass author = "agent" on scenarios its agent proposes); @approved_on in place of @revision, and current_approved(); @spend_basis; check_budget(); and the two additions below, both now built.
  • Since 0.4.0. The master-plan verbs: match_rows() in place of any row matching of its own, assign_sections() for the organization tree, ops_within() to enforce a planner’s scope before building, and rebase_check() before replaying a draft onto the current revision.

Two package-side additions would make that integration deterministic rather than prose-steered, and belong here because the app’s own charter says all plan semantics live in mediaplanr:

  • describe_plan(plan) → a plain list: grain, each grain column’s distinct values, the flight window, the line-item roster, units by type, and totals. The app has a describe_plan tool that rebuilds this by hand; making the package’s version canonical means the model and R cannot drift apart. Phase 1 and 3 already deliver the pieces, and the subplan map is now subplan_map() — built on the same argument, along with ownership_map(), lineage() and plan_mermaid(): projections the package owns so a renderer cannot drift. Anything that needs a graphics dependency belongs in the companion, mediaplanr.viz, which draws only from these projections. Built — capped rather than a full roster, so it fits an agent’s context at any plan size; see Already grown. The app has not adopted it yet.
  • plan_ops_schema() → the JSON Schema for the operations array. The app passes ops to the model as an unschema’d JSON string, because ellmer’s typed arguments cannot express the recursive shape, so a malformed op is discovered only when R throws. Built — see Already grown; the app has not adopted it yet.

Serialization to JSON

A plan crosses the app boundary — saved, reloaded, handed to a model — so it needs a JSON form. This is smaller than it looks, for the same reasons the copy helper in revise() is: the class stores a flat table and a handful of scalars, and everything else is derived.

Decided

Serialize the settable slots, nothing derived. The write side filters MediaPlan’s properties to the settable ones — the exact getter filter the revise() copy helper uses — and emits those plus a schema_version:

ps       <- attr(MediaPlan, "properties")
settable <- names(ps)[vapply(ps, function(p) is.null(p$getter), logical(1))]
# @data, @grain, @time_col, @time_basis, @id, @parent_id, and the metadata scalars

flight_window(), pacing, week_start() are not written. They are recomputed on load, which keeps the JSON small and — more importantly — makes it impossible to persist a stale derived fact, the same rule that keeps them off the class.

Read back through media_plan_from_df(), not the raw constructor. The constructor round-trips, but the from-df door re-runs validation and re-solves the units identity, so a hand-edited or drifted file rebuilds clean rather than merely reconstructed. media_plan_from_df() already takes id and parent_id, so identity and lineage survive the trip — the rebuild is faithful, not fresh.

A schema_version from v1. The one thing that is cheap now and expensive later. It rides on the top-level object so the reader can branch on shape.

The encoding conventions, all minor. Dates have no JSON type, so the week column goes out ISO 8601 and is reparsed on load; auto_unbox collapses a length-1 grain and an empty parent_id becomes [], so both are coerced back to character on the way in. None of this is structural.

Subplans recurse, but only the writer gets it free. .plan_payload() derives its fields from the class’s settable properties, so @subplans is picked up with one recursive lapply so children are emitted as payloads. The key is omitted when empty, so a flat plan serializes exactly as it did; the parent’s @data is still written in full, so a reader that ignores subplans gets the right totals. schema_version went to 2, which also added revision.

The reader needs more than recursion. It rebuilds through media_plan_from_df(), which knows nothing of subplans, so children are rebuilt first and then attached through attach_subplan(), never assigned into the slot. A hand-edited parent row is corrected rather than trusted, and a file describing an illegal tree is refused with the same error an interactive attach gives. The reader is also the one place uncapped depth is a hazard — a written tree is finite, a parsed one need not be — so it carries a nesting limit of 32 with a clear error, a parser’s bound rather than a constraint on the model.

Flights needed no special path

The first worry here was flight identity: media_plan_from_df() looked like the wrong door for a flighted plan, so it seemed a reader would have to branch to the flights door on flight_id. It does not. The flight columns (flight_id, flight_start, flight_end, period_basis, pacing) live in @data, so they travel with it, and the validator accepts them once the two date columns are reparsed — no branch, no separate flights-door path. A mixed plan, where only some rows belong to an authored flight and the rest carry NA, rebuilds the same way. And media_plan_from_flights() forwards ... to media_plan_from_df(), which already takes id and parent_id, so lineage survives either door.

plan_to_json() and plan_from_json() implement this, covered by a round-trip suite over weekly, geo, units, flighted and mixed plans.

Already grown

Listed because earlier revisions of the README named these as future work:

  • Metrics beyond spend — built. unit_type, planned_units, planned_rate, bound by one identity, with the rate as the invariant under an edit.

  • Flighting — built. Plans can be authored as flights and are held as weeks; flights() inverts it exactly, and calendarize() re-cuts onto any calendar.

  • Adding and dropping line items — built, via the structural ops.

  • check_coverage() scoping on spans — built. It now selects rows through the same .row_span() every other date question uses, so it follows a flight that starts mid-week rather than the week it happens to sit in. The rule is overlap, which preserves every previous answer for weekly plans, and it is documented on ?check_coverage and in vignette("plan_concepts") — which was the actual gap, since the behaviour was defensible but unstated.

  • Serialization to JSON — built. plan_to_json() and plan_from_json() round-trip a MediaPlan or a whole ScenarioSet, through media_plan_from_df() so the rebuild is re-validated and lineage preserved; flighted and mixed plans need no special path. Covered by a round-trip suite and shown in vignette("getting_started"). The design reasoning is above, under Serialization to JSON.

  • SubPlans — built. One slot, no class: attach_subplan() replaces the cell’s rows with the subplan’s rollup and locks them, detach_subplan() releases them, is_topline() is the derived predicate, and a validator invariant holds parent rows equal to each subplan’s rollup so the two cannot drift. The subplan declares its cell through its data (same-or-finer grain, parent keys constant); calendarize() bridges cadence. revise() and the .copy_plan() door landed with it, closing the drop-a-slot trap, and JSON went to schema 2 with a recursive writer and a re-attaching reader. Depth is legal; one level is tested. The design reasoning is above, under SubPlans.

  • Op constructors and the ops schema — built. One registry in R/ops.R names every op, its fields and their types; .apply_op(), the op_*() constructors and plan_ops_schema() all read it, so they cannot disagree. A constructor returns the same plain list a hand-written or JSON op is, and every op – however it was made – gets the same plan-free checks when applied. With a plan, the schema narrows targets to its grain values and dates to its basis. The style reasoning is above, under API style.

  • transfer — built. The commonest real edit, a zero-sum move between line items, as one op rather than two deltas whose pairing is lost. Each side spreads like delta; a destination that plans nothing fills evenly by in-market days, the rule an even flight follows. All three of delta, total and transfer spread money through one helper, .distribute(), which is where spend bounds are enforced.

  • Spend bounds — built. Optional min_spend / max_spend per row (bound_cols()) record commitments, floors and caps; the validator holds min <= spend <= max to the cent. Group edits water-fill around a bound in .distribute(); per-row edits are refused at one; drop, shift and restage respect them; roll_up(), calendarize(), flight import and subplan rollups carry them. “Committed” / “floor” / “capped” is derived by .commitment(), never stored. Bounds change only through the rebound op. Line-total commitments (“$300K upfront, phasing flexible”) are group rules, planned with PlanConstraints.

  • Provenance — built. A derived plan carries @edits, the canonical record of what build_scenario() applied (ops operation-first with dates as text on the plan’s clock, or the allocation as given), and @rationale, who proposed it and why. The scenario is derived by replaying its own record, so replaying @edits on the parent reproduces it exactly; an added flight’s id is minted into the record for the same reason. Roots and rollups record none, nothing inherits it, revise() may set a rationale. edit_log() reads a set’s records as a change log. JSON went to schema 4.

  • describe_plan() — built. The agent’s view of a plan: identity and provenance, shape, spend by each line item column, commitments, units, spend by month, and what an op may target. Every list is capped at top_n values plus a counted remainder, so the description stays a few kilobytes at any number of rows (only the by-month section grows, with the plan’s duration), and every number reconciles to @data. Later phases add their facts to it.

  • Approvals — built. @revision is gone. A plan carries its approval as @status = "approved" and an optional @approved_on date (never defaulted from today; cleared when the status moves on; never inherited by a derived scenario or a rollup). lineage() derives each approved plan’s revision – its place among the approved plans on its branch – and flags the current one: approved, with nothing approved derived from it. current_approved() returns it, warning when parallel branches leave more than one and never breaking the tie by date. compare_scenarios() takes against = "base" | "parent" | "current_approved". Older JSON carrying revision reads with it ignored.

  • Spend basis — built. @spend_basis declares what planned_spend measures ("media_net", "client_net", "gross", or anything else; "" undeclared). Set at import or corrected with revise(); carried by scenarios and rollups. Plans combine – in a ScenarioSet, or as a subplan – only when their bases match exactly, undeclared included.

  • check_budget() — built. The envelope check: a budget table of windows and amounts, each naming any subset of the line item columns (or none), compared with the plan’s spend measured day by day through calendarize(), so a window may cut a week or month anywhere. Reports planned, variance and whether each row is within tolerance; a value the plan lacks reads as absent, not as an underspend. Warns, never errors, like check_coverage(). describe_plan(budget = ) summarises it. The help pages contrast an envelope (a target, with tolerance) with a subplan (ownership, with equality).

  • The model map — built (0.3.0). model_map() assigns every line item exactly one response model from a list fitted at mixed grains: of the models whose named values all match, the most specific wins; a tie is an error naming both, a gap is a warning with the unmodeled share. spend_by_model() sums each model’s spend by period through calendarize(), keeping unmodeled spend under model_id = NA so totals reconcile. Data frames in and out; no dependency on mrmopt. describe_plan(models = ) reports coverage.

  • The constraint object — built (0.3.0). PlanConstraints holds the group rules a plan lives under – min/max spend, min/max share, a fixed total with free phasing, max change (absolute or %) from a reference plan – built from rule_*() constructors or a rules sheet, kept one canonical way, with a constraints_schema() for agents and a JSON round trip. Row rules stay spend bounds on the plan. check_constraints() measures each rule day by day (like check_budget()) and reports actual, limit, slack and ok, warning on a violation and never refusing one; change rules need a reference. describe_plan(constraints = ) reports the broken and the binding rules, and a scenario’s rationale$constraints_id names the rule set it was checked against.

  • Sections and scopes – built (0.4.0). match_rows() is the public face of the edit path’s matcher: one target or a list of targets, during, strict or lenient. assign_sections() places line items in an organization tree’s leaves, reporting overlaps and gaps without refusing them. ops_within() checks a list of ops against a scope in order, so an add creates rows a later op may target. rebase_check() compares the rows a draft touches on its base and on the current revision. regrain() adds an organization level as a grain column. The reasoning is above, under Sections and scopes.

Not yet built

  • mrmopt reading PlanConstraints — the next cross-package step, so the optimizer and the agent’s self-check enforce the same definition of “allowed”. check_constraints() documents the semantics it must match: spend measured day by day inside each rule’s window, shares against the whole plan in the same window. Not started here; mrmopt is untouched.
  • regrain() beyond one flat plan. It takes one plan: a set of revisions and drafts is regrained plan by plan with the same arguments (ids, and so lineage, are unchanged), and a topline is refused because its subplans would need the column too.
  • A spreadsheet importer, as a companion package (mediaplanr.io): a declarative column map plus regex rules that turn an agency workbook into a MediaPlan and a lint report. A companion so that readxl and the long tail of workbook conventions stay out of this package.

Deliberately not planned

  • A channel-type registry / media taxonomy. The package hard-codes no column name anywhere. channel is a dimension a user happened to key on, and plans keyed on media_type or vehicle are equally valid.
  • Attribution, response curves, forecasting, optimization. These live in the mrmopt engine. An earlier revision of this package included a forecast() and an optimizer; both were removed for reasons written down in vignette("plan_concepts") and should not be rebuilt by accident.
  • Anything derived from Sys.Date() — weeks_remaining, is_active, pct_delivered. The rule the package holds: if a value can change without the plan changing, it does not belong on the plan. This is what keeps the flight window legitimate and these out.
  • Fee schedules and spend-basis conversion. @spend_basis declares what the figures measure; it never converts one basis into another. Turning media net into client net means applying an agency’s fee schedule, which differs by contract and by channel. That belongs in the caller, or in a companion package, not in the plan.
  • Ids as an external join contract. @id, @parent_id and flight_id are opaque, exist for identity and lineage, and are scoped to a derivation tree. Do not build an external join on them.
